title: Space & Cosmos Shorts · Episode 1
chapters: Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep

units.t: Space & Cosmos Shorts. Episode one.
In this episode: Auroras and space weather, Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep, First Nations astronomy and Pluto and the dwarf planets.
Part one. Auroras and space weather.
The southern lights are a solar storm hitting Earth's invisible shield, and the same storms can knock out power grids and drag satellites from the sky.
Light from the Sun.
In May 2024, people across southern Australia stepped outside to find the sky glowing pink and green.
The aurora australis, or southern lights, was seen far further north than usual during one of the strongest geomagnetic storms in about two decades.
Auroras usually hang around the polar regions, in curtains, arcs and rays roughly 100 to several hundred kilometres up.
Their northern twin is the aurora borealis.
Both begin at the Sun.
Its corona, over a million degrees, boils into space as the solar wind, charged particles streaming outward at hundreds of kilometres per second and usually reaching Earth in a few days.
Solar activity rises and falls over roughly 11 years.
The latest maximum, around 2024 to 2025, is why so many Australians saw auroras.
Earth's invisible shield.
Earth is protected by a magnetic bubble, the magnetosphere, generated by molten iron churning in the outer core.
The solar wind squashes it on the Sun-facing side and stretches it into a long tail on the other.
Most of the solar wind flows around it.
But magnetic field lines dip into the atmosphere near the magnetic poles, and energy stored in the magnetosphere can drive charged particles down along them.
That is why auroras form in rings, called auroral ovals, around both magnetic poles.
When the solar wind is calm, the southern oval sits over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean.
When the Sun hits hard, the ovals expand towards the equator, and Tasmania and the mainland get a show.
Why the colours differ.
An aurora is a little like a neon sign.
Fast particles slam into atoms and molecules of air, giving them energy, which they release as light.
The colour depends on which gas is hit and how high up it is.
Oxygen around 100 to 250 kilometres up gives the most common colour, a vivid green.
Higher still, where the air is extremely thin, oxygen can glow deep red, which is why great storms often paint the top of the sky crimson.
Nitrogen adds blues and purples, often along the lower edges.
Our eyes are poor at colour in dim light, so a faint aurora can look pale grey.
A camera gathering light for several seconds often reveals colours you couldn't see.
When the Sun storms.
When tangled magnetic fields near sunspots snap and reconnect, they release enormous energy.
A solar flare is an intense flash of radiation reaching Earth in about eight minutes.
A coronal mass ejection, CME, is a vast cloud of magnetised gas, billions of tonnes of it, usually arriving one to three days later.
If its magnetic field lines up the right way, it can spark a geomagnetic storm.
The largest on record, the Carrington Event of 1859, sent auroras far into the tropics and made telegraph systems spark and fail.
In March 1989 a storm induced currents in Quebec's power grid, and millions lost electricity for hours.
In February 2022, SpaceX lost dozens of new Starlink satellites after a modest storm increased drag on them.
Storms can also scramble radio and GPS.
Chasing the southern lights.
Tasmania is Australia's aurora capital, but strong storms can bring displays to Victoria, South Australia, southern New South Wales and southern Western Australia.
Get well away from city lights, ideally somewhere with a clear, low southern horizon such as a beach or hilltop.
A cloudless, moonless night helps enormously.
Auroras can appear at any time of year, often around the middle of the night, and can surge and fade within minutes, so patience pays.
Sign up for alerts from the Bureau of Meteorology's space weather service, which also watches the Sun and issues warnings, or follow local aurora groups online.
Bring warm clothes and a camera set to night mode or long exposure.
Even a faint glow can photograph in vivid colour.
The key idea: Auroras are light shows high in the atmosphere, triggered by the solar wind streaming from the Sun.
Part two. Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep.
For thousands of years comets were seen as omens of doom.
Then one astronomer predicted a comet's return, died before he could see it, and was proved right.
Omens in the sky.
A comet appears suddenly, hangs in the sky for weeks with a ghostly tail, then fades.
To many ancient cultures that unpredictability was frightening.
Chinese astronomers kept careful comet records for more than two thousand years, often linking them to political upheaval.
In 1066 a bright comet appeared over Europe shortly before the Norman conquest of England, and the Bayeux Tapestry shows people pointing at it in alarm.
The word comet comes from the Greek for 'long-haired', describing the streaming tail.
Aristotle believed comets were something happening in Earth's upper atmosphere, not objects travelling through space.
It took many centuries, and better telescopes, to prove him wrong.
Halley's bold prediction.
In the early 1700s, the English astronomer Edmond Halley studied records of bright comets and noticed that those seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had remarkably similar paths.
Using his friend Isaac Newton's new laws of gravity, he argued they were a single comet on a long oval orbit, returning roughly every 75 to 76 years.
He predicted it would reappear around 1758.
Halley died in 1742 and never saw the result.
On Christmas night 1758, a German farmer and amateur astronomer, Johann Palitzsch, spotted the comet right on cue.
It was a triumph for Newton's physics, and the comet has carried Halley's name ever since.
It last passed in 1986 and is due back in 2061.
A dirty snowball.
In 1950 the American astronomer Fred Whipple proposed that a comet's heart, its nucleus, is a 'dirty snowball' of frozen water, carbon dioxide, ammonia and other ices mixed with dust and rock.
Space missions have since confirmed the basic idea, though many comets turned out to be more dust than ice.
A typical nucleus is only a few kilometres wide and surprisingly dark, reflecting about as much light as charcoal.
When the European probe Giotto flew past Halley's Comet in 1986, it photographed a lumpy, peanut-shaped nucleus roughly 15 kilometres long, jetting gas from its sunlit side.
The display we see from Earth comes not from this tiny core but from the vast cloud it releases when warmed.
Two tails, not one.
Far from the Sun a comet is frozen and inactive.
As it swings closer, sunlight warms the surface and the ices turn straight into gas, dragging dust out with them.
This builds a fuzzy atmosphere called the coma, which can be larger than Jupiter.
Then the tails form.
The dust tail is pushed gently by sunlight, curves along the comet's path and shines yellowish white.
The ion tail is made of electrically charged gas swept away by the solar wind, so it runs straight and often glows blue.
Here is the surprise: both tails point away from the Sun, not behind the comet.
When a comet heads back out into the solar system, it travels tail first.
Origins and Rosetta.
Comets are leftovers from the formation of the solar system about 4.
6 billion years ago.
Those returning in under 200 years mostly come from the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
Comets with orbits of thousands or millions of years are thought to come from the Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy objects.
No one has directly seen it; it is inferred from the orbits of comets.
The European Space Agency's Rosetta reached comet 67P, a rubber-duck-shaped body about four kilometres long, after a ten-year chase.
In November 2014 it released the Philae lander.
Its harpoons failed to fire, and it bounced twice into a cliff's shadow, yet sent data for about 60 hours.
Rosetta found 67P's water differs chemically from Earth's oceans.
The key idea: Before science explained them, comets were widely feared as signs of disaster, and even Aristotle misjudged what they were.
Part three. First Nations astronomy.
Long before telescopes, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples read the night sky as a calendar, a map, a law book and a library of stories.
The oldest sky watchers.
Australia's First Peoples have lived on this continent for at least 50,000 years, and many researchers think longer.
For all that time they have looked up at the same southern sky, and their knowledge of it is woven through culture, law and daily life.
There is no single "Aboriginal astronomy".
Australia has hundreds of distinct nations and language groups, each with its own stories and ways of reading the sky, though some stories are shared across vast distances.
The stars were used to tell the seasons, find food, navigate, mark ceremonies and pass on rules for living.
Some of this knowledge is sacred and not for public sharing.
The Emu in the Sky.
Western constellations join up bright stars.
Many Aboriginal traditions also look at the spaces between them.
The best known example is the Emu in the Sky.
Its head is the Coalsack, a dark dust cloud beside the Southern Cross, and its neck, body and legs stretch along dark lanes in the Milky Way.
On autumn evenings, after dark, the emu appears to be running across the sky.
For a number of groups this coincides with the time emus are mating and laying eggs, a signal for when eggs could be collected.
Later in the year the emu's shape appears to change position, reflecting different stages of the breeding cycle.
The Seven Sisters.
The Pleiades, a small, tight cluster of stars, has inspired stories in cultures from ancient Greece to Japan.
In Australia it is the heart of the Seven Sisters, one of the most widespread and important Aboriginal stories.
In many desert versions, sisters are pursued across the country by a man, often linked to stars in the constellation Westerners call Orion.
As they flee, their journey creates and names features of the landscape, forming songlines: routes that link sites over thousands of kilometres and carry knowledge, law and ceremony.

In 2017 the National Museum of Australia staged Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, developed with Anangu, Martu and Ngaanyatjarra communities and sharing parts of the story through paintings, song and dance.
Tagai and star calendars.
For Torres Strait Islanders, the most important sky figure is Tagai, a great fisherman standing in his canoe.
In common descriptions, his left hand holds a fishing spear, the Southern Cross, and his right hand holds a sorbi fruit, the stars of Corvus.
His canoe and crew are made of other stars.
Tagai teaches the importance of following rules and sharing, and his position guides when to plant, fish and hunt turtle and dugong.
Across Australia, stars appearing at dawn or dusk signal events on the ground.
In the 1850s William Stanbridge recorded Boorong knowledge in north-western Victoria, including stars used to mark the seasons for gathering food.
These calendars are tailored to local country, since seasons differ across Australia.
Tides, eclipses and respect.
Sky knowledge was not only stories; it recorded careful observations.
The Yolngu of north-east Arnhem Land link the tides to the Moon, describing the Moon filling with water as tides rise, which captures a real connection.
Several groups have stories explaining eclipses, often as the Sun woman and Moon man coming together.
Researchers have found traditions that appear to describe changing brightness in stars such as Betelgeuse and Antares, which astronomy recognises as variable.
Some scholars think stories about Wolfe Creek Crater may preserve memories of real events, though that is hard to prove.
To learn more, seek sources made by or with communities, such as Aboriginal-run tours and museum resources.
Stories differ between nations, and some knowledge is restricted.
The key idea: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have read the night sky for many thousands of years, with knowledge that differs between nations.
Part four. Pluto and the dwarf planets.
In 2006 Pluto was voted out of the planet club.
The real story is less about Pluto being demoted and more about discovering it had a lot of company.
Found by patience.
In the early 1900s, astronomer Percival Lowell was convinced an unknown 'Planet X' lay beyond Neptune, and his observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, kept searching after his death.
In 1929 it hired Clyde Tombaugh, a 22-year-old Kansas farm boy with no university degree, who had impressed staff with drawings from his homemade telescope.
Tombaugh photographed the same patches of sky several nights apart and flicked between the plates with a blink comparator, looking for a dot that moved against the background stars.
On 18 February 1930 he found one.
The calculations that inspired the hunt later proved wrong, so finding Pluto was partly luck, combined with enormous patience.
Named by a schoolgirl.
News of the new planet spread worldwide, and name suggestions poured in.
In Oxford, England, 11-year-old Venetia Burney heard about it over breakfast and suggested Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld, fitting for a cold, dark world at the edge of the solar system.
Her grandfather passed the idea to an astronomer friend, who sent it to the Lowell Observatory.
Staff there voted unanimously in favour, partly because the first two letters, P and L, honoured Percival Lowell.
Venetia reportedly received a five-pound note as a reward.
Soon after, Walt Disney introduced a cartoon dog named Pluto.
Decades later, an instrument on the New Horizons spacecraft was named in her honour.
Smaller and smaller.
At discovery, Pluto was assumed to be roughly Earth-sized, because it was thought to be disturbing Neptune's orbit.
Each new measurement shrank it.
In 1978 astronomers discovered its largest moon, Charon, which allowed Pluto's mass to be calculated precisely.
It was tiny: only about a fifth of our Moon's mass.
Pluto is about 2,380 kilometres across, narrower than Australia is wide.
Charon is about half Pluto's diameter, so large that the two swing around a shared point in the space between them.
Pluto's orbit is also odd: stretched and tilted, and between 1979 and 1999 it came closer to the Sun than Neptune did.
A crowded neighbourhood.
In 1992 astronomers found another small icy body beyond Neptune, the first known member of what is now called the Kuiper Belt.
Hundreds, then thousands more followed.
Pluto was not a lonely ninth planet but one of the largest of a vast belt of frozen leftovers.
The crisis came in 2005, when a team led by Mike Brown announced Eris, first thought larger than Pluto.
Later measurements showed it is very slightly smaller in diameter but about a quarter more massive.
If Pluto was a planet, Eris had to be one too, and possibly dozens more.
In August 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet in Prague: it orbits the Sun, is massive enough to be round, and has cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.
Pluto has a heart.
Pluto passes the first two tests but fails the third, because it shares its region with countless Kuiper Belt objects.
It became a dwarf planet, alongside Eris and the asteroid Ceres, with Haumea and Makemake added later.
Some planetary scientists still argue for a definition based on a body's own properties, not its surroundings.
NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto on 14 July 2015, nine and a half years after launch.
Expectations were modest: an old, cratered ball of ice.
Instead it found a pale heart-shaped region, Tombaugh Regio, holding Sputnik Planitia, a young plain of nitrogen ice that flows like glaciers and has almost no craters.
There were also water-ice mountains kilometres high and a blue haze.
Some of Tombaugh's ashes were aboard.
The key idea: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by comparing photographs of the sky, partly through luck and mostly through patience.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the solar wind?
Answer. Charged particles streaming out from the Sun.
Question two. How did many ancient cultures see comets?
Answer. As frightening signs of disaster.
Question three. Why is there no single 'Aboriginal astronomy'?
Answer. Hundreds of nations have their own sky stories.
Question four. How did Clyde Tombaugh find Pluto?
Answer. By comparing photographs for a dot that moved.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
